cues: We start off today with Sam who's going to first talk about the state and the
future of the KERI suite. All right. Thank you. You guys.
And since we're recording, if you want to ask a question, we'll pass around the mic
so that your question gets on the recording. We have a couple of mics. I
recognize most of the people here, but there's some that I don't. Is there
anybody here that has never heard of KERI before other than to come to this
conference. Okay. Everybody's heard of KERI. Is there anybody here that just
really doesn't know that much about KERI? Oh, come on. All right. A couple. Okay.
KERI is sometimes described as complicated and I like to say it's no more
complicated than it has to be to achieve the properties that it provides. It's
designed to be minimally sufficient to achieve those properties. But those
properties are significant and difficult to achieve. If
something is confusing or something like that, part of this conference is to try to
explain those things. The KERI Foundation has been publishing videos of a lot of the
talks. We now have a fairly big set of videos that you can go watch and learn
from. And every time we do a presentation or a mini conference, we're attempting to
add to that corpus of knowledge there. I want to talk a little bit about KERI.
2026, we think is a milestone year for KERI and ACDC and the KERI suite of
standards and there's some reasons for that. Some things that have already
happened this year. We first had the suite of protocols released as a Linux
Foundation set of standards. We finalized the specs. It took several years to get to
that point and some of the people that were instrumental in getting there are
here today. Thanks for all that. The KERI Foundation was founded in 2025, but
we received funding, both private and public funding to start building open
infrastructure for KERI. We got a grant from the state of Utah Governor's Office
of Economic Opportunity. The telecom industry is using KERI and ACDC to stop
call spam. There is something called the Open Verifiable Communications Alliance and
that is functionally
in production. Microsoft has gone public and announced that they're using a
software stack developed by company called Provenant to solve call spam.
That's just growing organically that eventually call spam will be a thing of
the past. Five years from now, people won't be complaining about call spam.
That's how significant that is. And that includes text as well. It's going to
go into text. The Utah State passed a legislation, Senate Bill 260, that
implements what's called state-endorsed digital identity. That's a first. No one's
ever done that before. It passed both houses unanimously. It's a significant
achievement. Lots of states have been trying to do various forms of digital
identity and have been unsuccessful. The reason Utah State's passed is because the
digital identity was based on constitutional principles as opposed to
other principles. Some other things. There's a vital initiative in the
healthcare industry and actually that's now deepened GLEIF and DirectTrust.
DirectTrust is the organization that vets health information service providers and
also certifies certificate authorities and that issues certificates and identities in
the healthcare industry. They are going to issue, they are going to become a
qualified vLEI issuer. I can't… – Qualification agent. – Qualification
agent, which will then qualify
qualified vLEI issuers. This is an example of deepening and extending the
organizational density Root of Trust that GLEIF provides that was the early adopter
of KERI now to a sector that is the largest single market sector in the United
States, the healthcare sector. And they've done some proof of concepts pilot
projects and now have large payers like CVS I don't know if you know how big CVS
is, but revenue is the same size as Microsoft. It's not worth as much as
Microsoft because it's not a high-tech company, but that's how big it is. It's
now starting to use that to connect payers to payers and participants in the
healthcare industry. There was a summit earlier this spring at Utah State where a
significant amount of intention was drawn to the SEDI project. We had the first ever
KERI conference. Some of you attended it. Those who did attend
it, you'll get some of what was at that conference today, much reduced because the
KERI conference was two days with multiple tracks. This is one day with one track. We
released open source infrastructure, witnesses, watchers, and wallets and
continue to develop those. And I think and we'll be shortly releasing observers and
registrars. This is the KERI MiniConf. And in two weeks in Utah will be the fall
SEDI Summit, which will have about 250 participants. And there is an anticipation
that there will be multiple states that will announce their participation in a
multi-state SEDI consortium. Those are significant things that have happened just
in 2026. 2027 looks to be even better. To give you a little bit of history,
from my perspective, the journey down this KERI Suite path started for me back in
2013 and 2014 when I developed an open source, end-to-end encrypted and signed
communications protocol called RAET, Reliable Asynchronous Event Transport. The
insight that I learned from the development process is the key management
was the problem. I could do all sorts of things, but the key management was always
a sticky thing that I like we didn't really work. The key management, if
the key management is not done right, it doesn't matter anything else we do. The
protocol will fail. I then worked on something called the open reputation
system, published a couple of white papers, and that's where I identified that
persistent identity was the hard problem of identity. People were building and
people still do. Most of identity is not are not persistent or perpetual
identities. They're ephemeral identities and it's easy to build ephemeral identity.
It's really really hard to build persistent identity. I didn't know how to
build it. I knew that I needed to build it and so I started down that path. And then
I started publishing some white papers as part of Evernym and the Sovrin
Foundation on this path to perpetual identity. That takes us to 2016, 2017,
I call it the era of the ledger wars. Everybody decided that digital identity
based on blockchain was the coolest thing. And one of the things that blockchain does
is it does give you a form of perpetual identity. You can put the key state on the
blockchain so that you can maintain control over an identifier indefinitely
using the blockchain as your root of trust. The problem is everybody had their
own ledger and everybody wanted that identity be on their ledger. And as great
as the idea of Sovrin was, and we have founders of Sovrin here, everybody
said, well, it's too great an idea. We don't just want one ledger for identity.
We want every ledger to have their own identity. And that meant that you didn't
have interoperability. You didn't have portability and just created a host of new
problems. And those are all governance problems. I call that the ledger war
period. And I have lots of scars from that war because I spent several years fighting
that war and actually GLEIF adopted KERI because they fought that war and they
retreated off from the battlefield and said, we don't want to be on that
battlefield. We want a ledger agnostic approach to identity. We
have it here and we have Phil's here too. I pointed out Timothy, but Phil
was the founding chairman of Sovrin. We have some of the original ones there.
The result of that was that in 2018, they started developing, actually solving
the problem that identified years before, which is the hard problem, which is key
management. Wrote a white paper on fault tolerant key
rotation. And then started looking at building ACDCs with… if you had perpetual
identity, then you could have perpetually verifiable issuances and ACDCs did that.
And published the first KERI white paper in 2019. The core result of that white
paper was you didn't need blockchain to have perpetual identity. You could do it
securely without a blockchain. And that was a heretical concept at the time. I
remember every time I talked about that, the blockchain bros would beat me up and
just say, no, no, no, you got to have a blockchain, right? I fought, I have a
lot of battles from that fight, right? And then after a year of having the paper in
the wild and getting lots of feedback and finding all the mistakes and bad things, I
revised it and came out with version two, which is essentially what KERI is today.
There have been more incremental improvements since 2020, but the core KERI
idea hasn't changed much since the version 2 white paper. And the version 2 white
paper went through multiple iterations over the period of the next couple of
years, but they were small things. Quantum Secure DIDs was a paper published in 2020,
which is how we solve the ability
to basically be protected from surprise quantum attacks. That provides surprise
quantum attack protection, which means that we've pre-migrated KERI identifiers
today are pre-migrated to be protected so that you can migrate to post-quantum
secure things, but your existing identity is protected from a surprise quantum
attack. In 2020, late 2020, GLEIF work began. In 2020, published a white paper on
universal identifier theory which talked about how you solve organizational
identity with KERI.
We started the Trust over IP (ToIP) task force for ACDCs in 2020. A lot of these protocols
got started in that day. And then in 2022, GLEIF vLEI went into production. That
was the origination of it. And then since then in 2023, I wrote a white paper called
SPAC, which has now resulted in the trust spanning protocol. And we have Wenjing Chu,
the co-author there, and it's now in final draft. We voted on it, right? It should
go to spec. This is the fourth spec in the suite of protocols. Although usually
you don't think of a trust spanning protocol as a KERI suite of protocol, but
it solves the communication
metadata surveillance problem, which is what you need to start using some of these
things in different applications. 2023, as I mentioned, SEDI work begins. It
took three years. I was appointed to the Utah State Privacy Commission back in
2023, and we spent time trying to figure out how to get legislation through the
system. It wasn't an overnight thing. It's not like in January of 2026, some
legislators showed up and said, well, I have a bill. It's called SEDI. Let's vote
on it, right? That's a result of three years work of setting up the legislation.
And there are other people in the room that were essential in doing
that. And then 2023 is part of that work I wrote a white paper on sustainable
privacy. And then we formed the ToIP KERI Suite Working Group to get the specs
finalized. The Cardano Foundation adopted KERI. We have some of the Cardano. Well,
I guess they're Veridian now, right? Cardano has spun off a company called
Veridian. They're here. And then in 2025 was the first legislation where we did
digital identity rights. And then the KERI Foundation was established at the end of
2025. And then as I mentioned before, the Linux Foundation standards went final in
2026. That's sort of how we got started. A lot has happened and
it's happening faster. The rate is accelerating and it's been
it's challenging to keep up with it all. But everybody that's helped get it to this
point, I think there's a real sign that it's going to stick and it's going to
build because it does some things that nobody else can do. And I know we have
some people in here that maybe think other identity systems are great. I'm going to
be biased. I'm going to think no other identity system is anywhere close to KERI
and ACDC, right? But at least I'll make a good argument for it, right? Even if you
disagree with me. We started with cryptographic agility from the beginning.
It had to be everything is 100% cryptographically agile at the granular
level. I don't know of any other identity system that started with cryptographic
agility as a first order property of the whole system. The CESR protocol is
how we attain that cryptographic agility, which means that we're future-proofed. New
crypto comes along. We don't have to start from scratch. Anybody's… I mean,
the people behind Git and GitHub and the various organizations that use Git
have a difficult problem because it uses SHA-1 which is broken. But there's so much
code based on SHA-1 and there's no cryptographic agility that people have
tried to move it to SHA-2 or SHA-3 and they can't because there's just the lift
is too heavy. They keep patching it around it. But fundamentally, if they had
built it with cryptographic agility, they could have just switched to a different
hash and not have to change any of the tooling. You get that for free anytime
you build stuff on top of the KERI suite of protocols. Cryptographic agility is
baked in everywhere. Fault tolerant key management. The answer to security is not
more crypto. The answer to security is not more sophisticated mechanisms and
protocols. The answer to security is to fix key management. And the only way you
can fix key management is to make it fault tolerant because you can't make it
perfect. Every type of crypto has side channel attacks that are viable.
No matter what you do, you will fail at some point. The only way that it
actually will work is if you make it so that it's fault tolerant. A lot of
times this is a difficult concept. It takes a time for some people in the
security industry to understand that you really want to build things with fault
tolerance using first principle fault tolerance. A lot of people hear the
term fault tolerant and a lot of people in the blockchain world are familiar with a
brand of fault tolerance like Byzantine fault tolerance, but in the
critical systems infrastructure world, in the reliable engineering world, in the
survivable engineering world, these are worlds that I came from. I spent years in
those worlds before I ever looked at identity. The building systems that are
fault tolerant as a principle design… there are a well-known set of
techniques. What I did is I took those techniques and I applied them to key
management. And once I applied them to key management, all of a sudden key management
became a solvable problem. The first solution is you have identity that
is perpetual. And it's perpetual because under the hood, it's fault tolerant. If I
have a secure enclave like on my phone and I store my private keys in the secure
enclave, it's a piece of hardware. It's really, really hard to get to those
private keys. But it's not impossible. If I don't have a way to recover from
losing those private keys, my identity is only survives as long as the first exploit
of my private keys. And then once I lose my private keys, I have to start over.
It can't be perpetual if I can't recover from a compromise. I have to build
compromise recovery into my system. The very first thing we did is we assume in
KERI that your signing keys will be compromised. It's not like the blockchain
world where if your signing keys are compromised, you're done. It's a
catastrophic failure. That's what it means. If you lose your Bitcoin
address, your private key, then anybody can spend all your Bitcoin money and you
can't ever recover it. You're done. Done. We can't allow, we can't for identity that
is attached to a person, it has more value than the money in your bank account. It is
you. It is your identity that you want to control perpetually. It has to be fault
tolerant to the faults that are going to happen. The most likely faults and those
are your keys are going to get compromised. Your signing keys are going
to get compromised. Now that you have perpetual identity, you say, well, what am
I going to do with it? Right? I have an identity. I can improved control over
identity, but what am I going to do with it? How do you do things with it?
You issue things. People issue things to you. You issue things to other
people. You present things issued to you to other people. You need to have
issuances that have similar properties. You need issuances that are perpetually
verifiable. And the interesting thing is that if I have a mechanism that makes my
identity perpetual, I can use that same mechanism to anchor
and make issuances perpetually verifiable. We got a two for one. It's like we
built one set of infrastructure and it solved a whole other set of problems
without having to build additional infrastructure. We had to build some
additional infrastructure, but the core infrastructure we didn't have to rebuild.
And then we said, well, in the real world, if I'm going to do things with identity,
especially in organizations, I need delegation. Delegation wasn't an ad hoc
thing. Delegation is a first-order property of both KERI with delegated AIDs
and ACDC with edges and delegated issuances. We have two types of
delegation that can work synergistically. And they're not something that people like
right now this year, I'm seeing people talk about delegation in all sorts of
identity contexts. We were talking about delegation since 2020. We've been
talking about delegation for six years and we have hardened the concept of delegation
to where we know how it works, how to make it work and what to do with it. We're not
just inventing it this year. Lots of people are reinventing delegation this
year. I'm seeing lots of examples of, well, how do you do delegation? It's like,
no, no, we've been doing it for six years. And delegation, the same mechanism that
allows you delegation, allows you to do any kind of relationship. It doesn't have
to be a delegation relationship. It can be any kind of relationship and that
relationship can be provable, secure, verifiable, all of those properties. And
we have six years of doing that. KERI is no half measures for security. We don't
compromise on security. We go all in on we're going to make this as secure as you
can practically make it.
Another way to think about what KERI and ACDC do, I call the four A's of data
value, right? The whole point of doing this is to have data that's more valuable,
to be able to exchange data that's valuable. The first thing in the four
A's is it's authored. You want to be able to have a stable source of that
information that you can, that that who authored that data. You want to
then be able to authenticate the data and know that it came from that author. You
can securely attribute it. That means that everything that everybody does in the
ecosystem, they can be accountable. Now, you don't necessarily have to make it
accountable to a person or an entity. It can be accountable just to the identifier
and the identifier can have some degree of privacy associated with it, but it's still
accountable to the identifier. And this is important when you get into the agent
world because agents are these things that are operating, but who's accountable for
what the agent does? Is the agent accountable? This question came up
this morning as we were driving here. I noticed we passed, I think it was seven
Waymo autonomous vehicles that did not have drivers, right? When I was here
last spring, I didn't see that many. There was like seven just in like a mile. And
Caleb asked me the question, so if the Waymo gets pulled over, who does the
policeman issue the ticket to?
Who's the accountable party for that agent that's driving that car? If you can't
solve the accountable party problem, you can't practically have agents in the real
world because they're things. They're not people. Our whole legal system, our whole
society is based on the fact that people are the accountable agents. You
have to associate agents with the people that hold the liability. You have to make
them accountable. Authorized, authority chains, accountability by reference,
chains of authority. All of those things are part of making information valuable
when you're talking about permitting things to happen with data. And then
finally, authoritativeness. Can you trust the data? Is it reputable data? Is the
information there something that has value? And often we can't reproduce the
process of determining whether a statement has veracity. We can say, well, we know
who said it, but we don't know if they're lying when they said it. We just know who
said it. How do we trust the data? One of the ways you trust is by reference,
by reputation. If somebody that I trust says that you can trust Alice, if I trust
Bob and Bob says, I know Alice, you can trust Alice, then I trust Alice by
reference. And so much of trust in the real world, the bootstrap of trust comes
by reference. For example, GLEIF is a global root of trust for the ultimate
beneficial owner of a legal entity and the roles of the people that run the
organization and the roles of any of the members of the organization. And you trust
because you trust by reference. And if you can trust by reference, and
you can securely attribute and do the other ones above it, then you have a basis
for trust. […]
– I just wanted to point out there's a recursive element here too
because knowing that the reputation is trustworthy all goes back to the start
from the authored part and goes back in. – you can't have reputation if you
don't have the other ones. And then once you have reputation, then you can start to
trust the authoritativeness of the information. Like I have a PhD, right? And
so you would say, well, I can trust you because you have a PhD. Why can you
trust me? Because the institution that granted the PhD was accredited to
grant PhDs. Now, if you said, well, I'm going to tell you how to, I have a PhD.
I'm going to tell you all about how
to make explosives. And you might go, well, wait a minute. What's your PhD in? I
say, well, it's electrical computer engineering. I don't think they
teach electrical computer engineers how to make explosives. That would be like a
chemical engineer. Already the authoritativeness
of what I say is a function of the reputation that tells you whether or not
there's some basis for trusting me. Right? Without this ability to security
attribute up the chain to have reputation and systems of reputation, we don't have a
basis for trusting data that comes in over the internet. And we certainly can't trust
agents that are operating electronically without that. We have to solve that
problem. The mission of the KERI Foundation is to foster open
infrastructure. It's the I in KERI. There's a reason KERI is infrastructure.
Because to solve the perpetual identity problem in a fault-tolerant way requires
infrastructure. There's no way to solve it without infrastructure. But we want to
minimize that infrastructure. We want to make that infrastructure work in a certain
way. I use the phrase, I use the acronym DKMI for decentralized key
management infrastructure to describe what KERI is. KERI is a decentralized key
management infrastructure. It's a set of protocols that allow you to do that. And
it was designed to be web scalable to solve the cost floor problem of blockchain.
They said, well, blockchain is way too expensive. The cost floor is way too high,
right? We want it to be web scalable. We want an ultra low cost floor because it's
infrastructure and infrastructure costs money. It's not free. You want to at
least use infrastructure that's as cheap as the cheapest possible infrastructure
right now is web scale infrastructure. That was a design decision because we
couldn't get away from it. A lot of people have complained about KERI and said, well,
it's too complicated. You got to have witnesses. You got to have watchers.
That's too much. I want an identity that doesn't have that infrastructure. Well,
you can have an identity that doesn't have that infrastructure, but you can't trust
it. It's not secure. It doesn't satisfy the minimal properties. You either
decide that you're going to live in a world where you're hacked continually or
you're going to build the minimal amount of infrastructure that need to be secure.
And I can't think of any less infrastructure than a web-based open
source open standard things
that run at web scale. The idea is that we have a cooperative model so we can get
meta network effects. I wrote a white paper on meta network effects which says
that if you're sharing value that transfers across trust domains that you
get a meta network effect of that value. Reputation and the four A's of
data, all of those things are about secure attribution, identity. Those are all
things that move across trust domains. It doesn't matter. It's like I use this
example.
Reputation, some really good people have talked about reputation as being three
things. It's competence, honesty, and reliability. If I can trust somebody, I
have three reasons to trust or not trust. Somebody can be very competent, but if
they're not reliable, I can't trust them. Somebody can be very reliable, but not
competent. Like I have a younger brother who's an engineer. He's really reliable.
He's really competent in engineering, but I would not trust him to do open heart
surgery on me. Now, he actually has a son who's a doctor that I might trust to do
open-heart surgery on me. He's not quite yet. He's just barely out of residency, so
he hasn't reached that point yet. And then you have people and a lot of people think,
well, it's are they dishonest? Dishonesty is only one part of being
able to trust. What you want is those things that move across trust domains.
If I hire somebody to mow my lawn and they're reliable, like they show up on
time, they mow it, don't leave weeds, stuff like that. And then they come back
at the end of the season and say, hey, I'm starting a business where I'm going to be
shoveling snow. Okay. Right off the bat, I know that they're reliable. They
may not be competent at shoveling snow, although it doesn't take much to be
competent at shoveling snow. Would I trust them? I would trust them a lot
more than somebody who was not reliably mowing my lawn, right? It's not a
single property that we have to worry about. But there are lots of things like
that do move across domains and a lot of them are identity-based. You can
reconstitute your control of your identity from any copy of your key event log. And I
haven't gone to any detail inside the things. But this is an important property
because it means that as long as there's some infrastructure out there and you lose
all of your copies of your key history, as long as somebody has a copy, you can
reconstitute it. That makes it portable,
right? It's truly portable. There's no wallet vendor lock-in. We have true
portability across all the infrastructure providers. We have non-cooperative key
custodianship. A lot of people that say, well, keeping my private keys is too
difficult. Grandma can't manage your private keys. If I have a keys
custodian that's managing on her behalf, I want to be able to have that management
happen and be able to move to a different provider without requiring the cooperation
of the original provider. If for some reason they die in a snowmobiling
accident and they lose all of my grandma's keys, I can still move to a different
custodian.
Witness pools with no common mode failure sources benefit everybody that uses them.
And then the watcher network makes it so that you can tag duplicity. It was an
interesting thing. I used the term duplicity, but that was the biggest aha
moment in writing the KERI white paper is that if I can make every fault exhibit as
duplicity, then all I need is one mechanism. I need a duplicity detection
mechanism and now I can detect all faults. And the key to fault tolerance is you have
to detect faults. One of the in my early days, I attended a seminar by the original
team that was working on the Mars lander. And we were talking about they were
talking about a fault tolerance. Like the seminar went to a conference and I was
working on autonomous underwater vehicles, which aren't as cool as a Mars landers,
but they're still pretty cool. Right. Anyway, I was trying to learn from them
and they said and so the whole thing was about fault tolerance. It's like
how to build fault tolerance systems, how they put fault tolerance in the Mars
lander. And the key insight they said is we realize that we just can't
build any system that we can afford to put on a rocket and ship across space that is
imperfect, that is impervious to failure and impervious to fault. There's always
going to be faults that we can't account for. We just can't build them all in. But
they said, but what we could do is we could build a system that never failed to
detect a failure. We can't prevent it from failing, but we can certainly always
detect the failure. And then if we have enough time and resources, we might be
able to recover from failures. And I don't know if you pay attention to the early
days of the Mars Lander, but they recover from pretty severe failures. They had a
botched software upgrade and the system just like didn't work. And then they
figured out that if they did some things, stuff like that, they could boot it
in a particular mode where they could download a recovery program and
they were eventually able to recover it so the point is detect failures.
Build failure detection as your first and most important piece of infrastructure.
Then you can build on top of that. Duplicity, once I only had one thing I had
to detect, then failure detection got easy. I just have to detect duplicity. I
force everything to look like duplicity. KERI is designed so that every bad
behavior that an attacker could successfully benefit from exhibits as
duplicity. The duplicity detection then detects it so I can recover from it
before they gain full control over my identifier. We have something called
the five W's and we're going to have some more talks about that. These are shorthand
for wallet witness watcher. Those are the three primary infrastructure
components. We have the web runs on the web and the wizard is smarts behind the
scene. Now we have two other ones that didn't fit in the five W's. These are
registrars and observers, but we'll say that they're part of the web
infrastructure and we'll talk about those. That's what KERI infrastructure looks
like. You see that it's always two parties, You have entity A and entity B.
Each party has their own set of infrastructure. The infrastructure that's
shared is the watcher network. Entity A controls their own witnesses. Entity B
controls their own witnesses, which means you can't trust them. The watcher
network observes duplicity and therefore you can trust them because you only trust
them as far as they're not duplicitous and as soon as they're duplicitous you stop
trusting. It solves the governance problem because in blockchain the watcher network
and the witness network are the same network. You then have to have shared
governance between entity and A and B. And if they don't agree to shared governance,

This is an introduction to KERI, the Key Event Receipt Infrastructure.
My name is Samuel Smith and I am the inventor of KERI. The reason I invented
KERI is because the internet is broken and I wanted to solve it. And so the problem
that KERI solves is called the universal secure attribution problem. Okay, what do
we mean by universal secure attribution problem? Well, universal means everywhere.
We want it to be solved everywhere. And secure means do it in a way that can't be
hacked or forged or impersonated or attacked in the normal way that we get
attacked on the internet. Attribution means assigning a communication to its
source. We want to attribute where something came from to its source. We know
who's sending it to us. And so the problem is, how do we do that everywhere on the
internet in a secure way so that we know who's sending us information? So that
doesn't mean we want to enable anybody to track everybody's conversations. We want
to do it in a privacy protecting way. So that poses additional challenges. But
first we have to get the security down. Many people approach this problem and they
sacrifice security. And if you sacrifice the security, then you don't have privacy
either. So, what we want to do is solve all of these problems at the same time in
a very integrated, elegant, simple way. Let's talk about what it means. Secure
attribution is another way of saying we want to establish the authorship of data,
any and all data sent over the internet, any and all documents, things like
credentials, entitlements, authorizations. We want to be able to say that we can
securely attribute who's doing what in a privacy-preserving way. And I keep saying
privacy because I don't want to give the false impression that we're trying to
build this universal tracking system. The hard problem is to be able to do this all
in a way that keeps confidentiality and privacy along with secure attribution.
That's always been the hard problem. So to restate, the problem is we want to have
verifiable secure attribution of any communications to its source. Now I added
the word verifiable. What does verifiable mean? It means that if we're receiving
information, we need some way to verify where it came from. When I say verify, it
means in a cryptographic sense. It means doing it without having to trust any third
party. I don't want to have to trust somebody else to verify what somebody that
I want to communicate with in a private confidential way says. I need to be able
to do it by myself. If I have to trust someone, then the security of whoever I'm
trusting now becomes something I have to worry about. And that is a problem.
Another way of looking at secure attribution is to say that we want to have
provenance of any data by anyone, to anyone, from anyone. And so a way we can
describe that is as authentic data. And then we want authentic data provenance.
Authentic has two meanings. It means like true to yourself, like you're being
authentic. That's not the meaning of authentic we're using here. We're meaning
authentic as you can attribute it to its source. Who painted that painting is an
authentic painting, right? As opposed to when something's not authentic. It means
it was forged or somebody was impersonated. Somebody sends you
information and they say it came from Joe when it really came from Sue. And so the
whole problem is back to the same thing. We need to securely attribute the source
of information. So what do I mean by provenance? We often hear the term
provenance when we talk about like a painting, like fine art, right? Was it
painted by Rembrandt? And how do you know it was painted by Rembrandt? Well, one way
that you would provenance it is that you would establish a chain of custody of that
painting from Rembrandt to whoever Rembrandt sold or gave the painting to
whoever sold or gave the painting and so on. And if you can follow that chain of
custody to the present owner or holder of that painting, then you can say, yeah, it
came from Rembrandt. So if we can solve data provenance, then we can solve many of
the security problems on the internet because most of them come from the fact
that we can't solve data provenance. We don't have universal secure attribution.
And because we don't have universal secure attribution, people can forge things.
People can impersonate things. Well, when we send data over the internet, we have a
similar problem. Somebody sends a message. It gets sent to some server in the cloud
who then sends it to another server, who routes it to another server, who routes it
to another server, and then it ends up in your inbox. And you go, did it come from
where it said it came from? Anybody that was in the path could have intercepted it,
spoofed it, done something to it, and then it shows up in your box and it says, oh
yeah, this came from Sue, but it really came from Bob. So provenance is about
establishing secure attribution even though the data traverses multiple hosts
or servers on the internet. It didn't come directly to us. It wasn't given to us in
person. It came over the internet and the internet is public. The internet is public
infrastructure. It's public, which means that lots of people have the ability to
see what you're sending or to change what you're sending or to mess with it. And
many of the attacks on the internet come from the fact that it's public
infrastructure and therefore publicly accessible for attackers to attack. So we
want to solve this secure attribution problem. Let's dig a little deeper. On the
internet, we're just sending information. Data is information. It's just bits. Now
we talked about chain of custody. When we normally think of chain of custody, we
think of a physical item. So I'll call it those its. They're atoms. So if I actually
have a painting, there's only one of them. And it takes a lot of work to copy that
painting. And if I have two, then I have a problem because somebody made a copy. How
do you tell the original from the copy? Well, if the copy is done really, really
well, just looking at the two, you can't tell the original from the copy. That's
why you have to have a chain of custody. You say the original was in possession of
somebody and they gave it to somebody else and they gave it to somebody else. And the
copy was never in their possession. possession. So you know it's a copy
because it wasn't part of the chain of custody. That works for atoms. It doesn't
work for information bits. So we have a harder problem to provenance data
information. So we have to use cryptography to do that. One of the first
things we do with cryptography is that we give an identifier to the source. The
source now has an identifier. That identifier is an electronic identifier.
It's more information. It's more bits. To make the ability to security attribute to
a source, that identifier needs to be unique. And in order to have universal
secure attribution, that identifier needs to be universally unique. There can only
be one in the whole universe. The only way that we can guarantee your universally
unique identifiers is to use cryptography or to use some trusted third party who
creates them. Well, we don't want to have to rely on a trusted third party, so the
identifiers must be cryptographic in nature. So, let's suppose that we have a
system for generating cryptographic identifiers. Now, we must be able to prove
who controls that identifier, and we have to do it in a verifiable way without
trusting the third party. If I have a cryptographic identifier and a way to
verifiably prove controller over that identifier, then I have what is called a
root of trust. I have the ability now to attribute data to that identifier where
that identifier is the source of that data. So, I now have constructed the basic
